items.text:
The scallop dish at Amphora. | Alex Staniloff

This is Eater’s guide to all the new restaurants, bars, and cafes that have opened this week in September 2026. Throughout the month, we’ll update the list weekly (see: August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January). When we’ve been to a place, we will then include a few openings on our heatmaps (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, cocktail bars) to let you know the ones we like. If there’s an opening in your neighborhood that we’ve missed, let us know at ny@eater.com.

September 9

Spotlight

Flatiron: Amphora, a tasting room boasting one of the city’s biggest wine collections, opens on Wednesday, September 9, in the long-closed home of oenophile favorite Veritas. Executive chef Jack Logue (formerly of now-closed the Lambs Club and Betony) sends out three- and four-course menus, with a la carte options at the bar. Named for the ancient vessel used to transport wine across civilizations, Amphora is stocked with over 2,500 labels — making it one of NYC’s largest wine cellars. Wine director Chris Miller, a fellow Lambs Club alum, spotlights regions like Burgundy, Northern Rhone, Piedmont, and Champagne from top producers that include Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Coche-Dury, Raveneau, and Rousseau. 43 E. 20th Street, at Rutherford Place

And the rest…

Bed-Stuy: Mexican restaurant Olmo doubles down on the block with a collaborative new all-day taqueria and cafe called Peral. The team-up with Mexico City cafe and bar Cicatriz opened right next door to Olmo on Wednesday, September 2. Peral’s menu leans more casual than Olmo (see: tacos, many of which are guisados) with an affinity towards vegetarian and vegan options. 105 Saratoga Avenue, near Decatur Street

Chelsea: Vegan cinnamon roll bar Cinnaholic opened its first physical location in Chelsea over Labor Day weekend, inviting customers to jazz up gooey rolls with customizable toppings like fresh fruit, cookie dough, and chocolate drizzle. Coffee Project New York supplies the caffeine on-site. 228 Eighth Avenue, at West 22nd Street

Crown Heights: Brooklyn’s acclaimed Haitian patty pop-up Bon Pâtés debuted its first physical storefront over Labor Day weekend. Walk-up hours for its freshly baked patties are Thursday to Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., and catering and nationwide shipping are also still available. 637 Nostrand Avenue, at St Marks Avenue

Greenpoint: The owners of Wasabi, the Brooklyn sushi staple that closed this summer after a 26-year run, are back in the game with a new Japanese spot down the street. Ayune, which opened on Monday, September 7, specializes in hand rolls filled with the likes of tuna, salmon, shiitake mushrooms, or Japanese pumpkin, available in sets of three, four, five, or six ($19 to $38). Ayune takes over the former home of Botbar — a robot-run cafe with vegan food from Wasabi. At Ayune, expect a pared-down selection of Wasabi’s familiar favorites, owners Robby and Cristin Wijaya tell Greenpointers. While a beer and wine license awaits, Ayune serves nonalcoholic options like spicy mango coolers, yuzu shiso fizzes, lemonade, and teas. 664 Manhattan Avenue, between Norman and Nassau avenues

Long Island City: At Rewind — a 9,000-square-foot underground restaurant, cocktail bar, and karaoke lounge, which debuted on Wednesday, September 9 — diners enter by pressing a “rewind” button on an ’80s-style boombox that opens onto the bar. That’s where beverage director Ken Chen, formerly of Taipei’s Indulge Experimental Bistro, builds cocktails on tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Partner Alexander Lee’s menu includes truffle mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Beyond the restaurant are eight private karaoke rooms inspired by Hong Kong cinema, vintage recording studios, and other retro references. Rewind will also host a monthly guest bartender series featuring bartenders from New York spots like Stone & Soil, Yawning Cobra, and Red Sorghum. Rewind is co-founded by AYS Hospitality (behind NYC’s Mr. Moto’s collection of restaurants). 45-57 Davis Street, between Jackson and Skillman avenues

Lower East Side: Billed as “NYC’s most interesting sandwich shop,” ironically named Boring Sandwich opened inside a bodega on Saturday, September 5, with a globe-trotting assortment of gourmet sandwiches from chef Michael Brafman. The Shok-Shoe-Ka piles North African stewed tomato on an Aleppo bagel from Curly’s in Queens; a towering steak-and-egg Chivito pays homage to Uruguay’s national dish; and a New Orleans-styled muffuletta (a pressed Italian hero) also makes an appearance in the hidden dining destination that stays open until 10 p.m. Other orders include a tempura roll sandwich; chopped cheese riff; and another with Spam, tomato, crispy onion, and mala sauce. 97 Stanton Street, between Orchard and Ludlow streets

Soho: A new shop dedicated to single-source cacao with a bakery and cafe components, ÓOL, opened on Wednesday, September 9. Founder Ilana Gutierrez, who is from Mexico City, is showcasing single-origin cacao from Ecuador, Colombia, and Belize; it’s used for drinks with milks and/or water, along with spiced syrups like chile or ginger. ÓOL is partnering with NYC chain Breads Bakery for pastries made with that cacao, like a cacao swirl, cacao chop cookie, and a cacao croissant. In the near future, the two-story space will host tastings and workshops. 178 Spring Street, near Thomson Street

Tribeca: Keith McNally’s son, George, opened his first restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable. 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets

Tribeca: Evento, the nearly decade-old Italian hospitality company known for its cooking classes, culinary workshops, pasta-making dance parties, and big-ticket corporate events from Italian-born chef Andrea Belfiore and co-founder Sam Akiba, opened its first permanent home on Friday, September 4. The Manhattan flagship, housed inside the historic three-story Bogardus Mansion, is split up into three sections: a ground-floor cooking studio fit for pizza and pasta parties and workshops; a private dining room on the second floor dressed in Italian decor; and a forthcoming restaurant on the lower level. 75 Murray Street, between West Broadway and Greenwich Street

Upper East Side: Soba noodle house Kuriya, from the neighborhood team behind Japanese rice bowl restaurant Suki Desu, debuted on Sunday, September 6. Noodles presented on a tatami mat can be dipped in gyudon or topped with raw seafood, notes Infatuation. 219 E. 85th Street, between Second and Third avenues

Upper East Side: Bronx-born New York native, chef Lana Lagomarsini — a semifinalist on Top Chef season 22 and Gramercy Tavern alum — opens a supper clubby tasting menu spot centered on the Black culinary diaspora, on Wednesday, September 9. Creola, named after her grandmother, prepares courses like potlikker consomme (a nod to her grandmother’s collard greens) and oxtail pate en croute that riffs on the French pastry-wrapped meat dish. The $125 tasting menu is joined by $65 wine pairings. 1261 Park Avenue, between East 97th and 98th streets

Upper West Side: Derek Wu, the former manager of Lower East Side Chinese restaurant Wu’s Wonton King, heads across Central Park with the debut of Wu’s Dynasty on Thursday, September 3. As first reported by West Side Rag, the Cantonese newcomer is huge — it takes up 8,000 square feet — and does dim sum daily (with roving carts rolling around from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.). The parade of plates includes pan-fried Chinese chive and shrimp dumplings, pan-fried noodles with beef, cheong fun (steamed rice rolls), and custard lava buns. Live seafood and huge crustaceans like king crab greet customers upon entry inside tanks, and there’s Beijing duck, too. A bar serves cocktails, whiskeys, and wines. Hours run until 10 p.m. daily. 208 West 70th Street, between West End and Amsterdam avenues

Washington Heights: Eventually hoping to also be a bistro and bar, the ambitious new Boogie Lab opens as just an artisan bakery stocked with to-go loaves to start. “But this is just step one,” notes the team. Coming soon: food, drinks, music, and “an inviting space that shifts its rhythm from day to night.” 4015 Broadway, at West 169th Street

September 2

Spotlight

Midtown: After a revamp, iDen’s Beijing Duck House reopened on Tuesday, September 1, in its former La Grenouille space. The updated high-end duck restaurant originally opened in NYC last year, after its sibling location in Vancouver which had opened six years ago. The chef, Matt Chen, had run the kitchen of Le Palais in Taipei — apparently the first restaurant in Taiwan to receive three Michelin stars — retooled the menu, now featuring a $200 tasting menu as well as a la carte options like a duck-egg yolk roll; surf clam and okra salad; venison with Sichuan-pickled vegetables; and the Beijing duck, which starts at $128. 3 E. 52nd Street, between Fifth and Madison avenues

And the rest…

Chelsea: Showy clubstaurant STK Steakhouse has expanded its presence in the city, opening a spacious second location in Chelsea in mid-August. Diners — the space can fit 200 of them — will find the same steaks, seafood, cocktails, and “DJ-driven dining” (per a press release) that have kept the Midtown location going for nearly two decades. The restaurant will launch a seasonal pumpkin-focused menu beginning Wednesday, September 9, which includes offerings such as crab-stuffed shrimp in pumpkin cream sauce and pumpkin spice margaritas. The space was previously home to another flashy den of meat: Salt Bae’s Nusr-Et Steakhouse, which closed in 2024. 412 W. 15th Street, between Ninth and Tenth avenues

Chinatown: The team behind Essex Street’s old-timey photo booth Retrography unveiled a secret new cafe called Behind The Booth in the back on Wednesday, August 26. The slim-and-stylish setup specializes in an “unexpected” wine list and “ice cream you wouldn’t have ordered anywhere else,” per an opening message. 15 Essex Street, between Canal and Hester streets

Greenpoint: Acclaimed Lone Star pitmasters Jonny White and Chuck Charnichart brought Brooklyn a legit Texas barbecue joint on Sunday, August 30, with the opening of Kirbee’s. Their respective restaurants — Goldee’s in Fort Worth and Barbs B Q in Lockhart — are some of the best barbecue joints in the country over the last several years, with Michelin nods, James Beard nominations, and more. Charnichart’s barbecue plate features her South Texan and Mexican takes on barbecue: pork ribs with lime zest, brisket with Mexican spices, charro beans, and the iconic green spaghetti. White’s is more modern, with brisket, ribs, turkey, potato salad, and coleslaw. Each will include pickles and bread. Kirbee’s works like a true Texas barbecue: People line up outside the black-and-red storefront and place their orders at the first window; their orders will be cut up and plated inside; and then they’ll pick up their trays at the second window; after which they can either find a table in the 24-seat dining room. 55 McGuinness Boulevard South, between Engert Avenue and Newton Street

Greenpoint: Cozy corner coffee shop Loco Cafe opened in the small 500-square-foot space that was previously home to short-lived Viva La Pizza and Pizza Prince on Saturday, August 29, and the minimalist replacement inside has a winking cup of Joe logo. 626 Manhattan Avenue, at Nassau Avenue

Greenwich Village: The swanky martini destination Chateau Royale has been flipped into the more neighborhood-y Floradora, which opened on Thursday, August 27. The new menu features snacks such as mozzarella sticks and pigs in a blanket, alongside French dip sandwiches, burgers, disco fries, chicken paillard, two-layer oxtail lasagna, and more. (The drinks menu, meanwhile, leans into tiny ’tinis and other “sorta-’tinis.”) As owners Cody Pruitt and Jacob Cohen have told Eater NY, the flip was motivated by a desire to make the restaurant “more accessible, price-wise, as well as cuisine-wise, and vibe-wise, so we can see our neighbors more often;” diners at Chateau Royale tended to order the burger over the pricier Dover sole. It’s the second flip this summer for Pruitt and Cohen, who transitioned Libertine in the West Village into the “seafood tavern” Capitaine in June. 205 Thompson Street, at Bleecker Street

Upper East Side: Bright-orange Italian restaurant and pizzeria La Collina opened on Tuesday, August 18, for lunch, dinner, and brunch. Red and white pies join a namesake mozzarella salad and mains like Mediterranean sea bass with celery root puree or sirloin steak surrounded by roasted potatoes, plus a coconut Negroni or limoncello elixirs at the bar. A $34 two-course lunch option during the week features thinly sliced eggplant followed by tonnarelli cacio e pepe or tagliatelle Bolognese. 1431 First Avenue, at East 74th Street

West Village: NYC’s summer of Thai food continues on Wednesday, September 2, with the debut of Hommali from a trio of friends from Bangkok. The contemporary new spot rooted in Thailand’s beloved jasmine rice also offers a tom yum seafood cocktail; dry-aged duck breast served with fermented chile sauce; and penang curry with beef cheeks. A bar with a knack for fermentation and infusions slings drinks like the Tomato — a take on the michelada and a spritz, which includes a Singaporean rice wine made with jasmine and sticky rice. 28 Seventh Avenue South, near Leroy Street

Williamsburg: Small Change, a new bar from the team behind the Last Resort in the East Village and One Trick Pony in the West Village, opened in June in the former location of Lady Jay’s (which occupied the space for almost 15 years). The large backyard remains ready for group hangs, now with an awning of plants. Happy hour runs from 4 to 7 p.m., featuring draft beers and well drinks for $5, plus other drink specials. The beer-and-shot combo runs $8 all day. 633 Grand Street, near Leonard Street

Williamsburg: Finally, Ugly Baby has returned, having opened its new location on Thursday, August 27, in the corner spot that once housed Emmy Square Pizza. The restaurant first opened in Carroll Gardens in 2017 and quickly picked up a fervent following, who praised the restaurant’s intensely spicy dishes and its commitment to southern Thai dishes that were, at the time, less commonly found in the city. The popular and beloved restaurant closed in the final days of 2024, citing that chef Sirichai Sreparplarn was “tired and just needs a long break.” Sreparplarn is still behind the new version of Ugly Baby, which will have double the capacity of the original location and will feature a wider range of dishes. In Ugly Baby’s absence, some of its former employees went on to open Hungry Thirsty in the same location; it also welcomed a Manhattan sibling last month, the fiery Hungry Spicy. 364 Grand Street, between Havemeyer Street and Marcy Avenue

Update, 4:09 p.m.: This article, originally published at 10:55 a.m., has been updated to correctly reflect iDen’s Beijing Duck House’s reopening status.

The veggie dumplings at Mimi Cheng’s. | Mimi Cheng’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in September
items.text:
The veggie dumplings at Mimi Cheng’s. | Mimi Cheng’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in September 2026. This list will be updated weekly (see: August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January), serving as a round-up of the dining and drinking places that have shuttered around the city. If a restaurant or bar has closed in your neighborhood, let us know at ny@eater.com.

September 4

Spotlight

East Village: Mimi Cheng’s serves its last dine-in dumpling on Friday, September 11, noting the lease was up at this sole standalone location. “While closing this storefront will be sentimental, it means we get to pour everything into what’s next,” per a closing statement. Over its 12-year run, the tiny shop evolved into a nationwide business found in Whole Foods’ freezer aisles, and the plan is to continue to scale operations apart from its physical digs. The team is currently fielding interest from bars, restaurants, hotels, events, arenas, and other retail stores looking to sell its dumplings. A menu collab with Brooklyn’s Pizza Loves Emily featuring dry-aged beef-stuffed dumplings marked its final days of sit-down service in September. 179 Second Avenue, between East 11th and 12th streets

And the rest…

Bed-Stuy: Brooklyn’s blue-toned coffee shop, the Bureau, quietly shut down this week, notes Bed-Stuy Stoop, saying the building was repossessed by the city and handed back to the landlord. Chef Ayo Balogun also owns popular places like Dept of Culture and Radio Kwara in the same Brooklyn neighborhood. The Bureau went through several iterations under the same owners over its 13-year run, first as a basic cafe called Civil Service (which had to close after a car crashed into its window in 2018). It later reopened as Council Cafe before ultimately becoming the Bureau three years ago. 279 Nostrand Avenue, at Clifton Place

Brooklyn Heights: After 30 years in Brooklyn, family-run grocer All in One Deli Mart, fondly known as Peas N’ Pickles, closed its doors for good. Owner Minki Lee previously cited a spike in property taxes and rent as the cause for the closure. The neighborhood grocer also offered a vast prepared foods section full of subs, soups, and sushi. 79 Henry Street, at Pineapple Walk

Williamsburg: Boil n Bite, Brooklyn’s seafood boil destination loaded up with clams, calamari, crab, fish and chips, surf-and-turf options, and more, announced its closure on Instagram on Thursday, August 10. 148 N. Seventh Street, between Berry Street and Bedford Avenue

September 4

Spotlight

East Village: Double Zero, the vegan pizza and wine bar from celebrity vegan chef and raw food advocate Matthew Kenney, permanently closed this week after 12 years. “We have made the difficult decision that continuing Double Zero is no longer financially sustainable,” per signage on the door flagged by EV Grieve, citing rising food and operating costs, the “realities of our lease,” and an overall slowdown in demand for vegan dining.

Double Zero specialized in personal wood-fired pies topped with shiitake bacon and nut-based cheeses like cashew mozzarella to go along with sustainable wines. Back in 2018, Kenney announced plans to bring the restaurant to Philadelphia, plus other places like Brooklyn, Boston, and Los Angeles; ultimately, however, those locations never materialized. The James Beard-nominated chef and cookbook author previously opened several meat- and dairy-free restaurants across the globe.

The brand has gone through several changes recently. In early 2025, Double Zero and Bar Verde merged into one restaurant called PlantMade, which offered a combination menu of vegan pizzas and Mexican fare. Earlier this year, Kenney rejoined the team as consulting chef and flipped Double Zero back to its original form and name in the space next door to the Second Avenue original. (Its very first name, 00 + Co., confused customers and was quickly changed.) 65 Second Avenue, at Fourth Street

And the rest…

Union Square: Max Brenner, the whimsical chocolatier that commanded long lines in its early days, closed on Saturday, August 29, after 20 years of catering to the touristy Times Square crowd. Built as a restaurant, chocolate retailer, and interactive dessert bar all in one, Max Brenner served crepes, choctails, pizza topped with chocolate chunks, sweet waffles, and decadent fondue. A Reddit user who flagged the closure noted a post-COVID slump in sales under new ownership. 841 Broadway, between East 13th and 14th streets

West Village: Korean chef Jihan Lee’s TBD Gimbap held its last week of service in late August. The pint-sized takeout strictly specialized in seaweed-wrapped gimbap like his mom used to make, rolled to order and filled with beef bulgogi, spicy carrots, and spicy pork. “This isn’t goodbye. It’s just this chapter closing so the next one can start,” writes Lee in a closing statement, adding that “more gimbap is coming.” The Masa alum is also a partner at next-door Japanese hand roll bar Nami Nori since 2019, which has since expanded to New Jersey, Florida, and Virginia. 31 Carmine Street, near Bleecker Street

items.title: Steal My Food Itinerary: A Long Weekend in Upstate New York
items.summary: I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live
items.text:
I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live in Brooklyn, so of course I have an upstate New York itinerary for you. My partner’s mom’s partner (yes) has a cabin in Accord, New York, that we’ve been lucky to house sit, and I’ve fully fallen in love with the Catskills. Over the past few months, I’ve been so grateful to escape for a few long weekends among the trees and the birds and the slightly cooler weather of the Hudson Valley.

When I tell people in the city about my trips upstate, they’re often surprised to hear me gush about the restaurants. And while I think you could make all your meals (the bounty at the farm stands and markets make cooking very dreamy up there) and still have a great time, I can also strongly make the case for a dining-focused trip. Here’s where to go.

Day 1: Friday

If you’re heading up from the city, there are a few transit options (a bus from Port Authority to New Paltz or Kingston, the Metro North to Poughkeepsie, Amtrak to Hudson), but you’ll want a car to get around once you’re in the Catskills. I journey upstate via a car, which we pick up in New Jersey; that means that I get to grab Corner Slice’s massive, pillowy garlic knots as a pre-trip snack. If you find yourself in the area, I recommend you do the same.

Lunch

Stop at Storm King Art Center to take in the outdoor sculptures or catch a concert (I saw Dev Hynes’ ensemble there this summer and it was one of the most beautiful shows I’ve ever been to). I know museum restaurants are better than ever these days, but readers of this newsletter would probably appreciate that you can bring your own food and picnic, so I say pack a lunch. Anything goes; I’ve seen Panda Express from the nearest rest stop in those fields.

Dinner

Drive a little farther north and you’ll hit New Paltz, your first introduction to the charms of Upstate. Grab dinner at Shorties, a self-described “bar for the whole family” that lives up to the premise with DJs every night and pinball. A kimchi-topped hot dog is my move, but yours could be green pozole stew, togarashi-rubbed wings, or prosciutto- and pepperoncini-topped nachos. For those who are driving, a bonus at this spot is that the N/A drinks are good, with fun ingredients like salted guava juice. If you’re staying for longer than a night or two and planning to cook, stop by the fishmonger Gadaleto’s for all your seafood needs, while you’re in New Paltz. And if you’re planning to climb, you can rent pads from Rock & Snow.

Drinks

I stay in the Accord area, where lodging ranges wildly, from cabin Airbnbs to a souped-up retro motel to the luxury hotel Inness. The latter has a lovely (but pricey) restaurant for a group. Take in the same vibe (and view of the sunset) right outside the restaurant from the outdoor bar, where you can sit on Adirondack chairs around the fire and pretend you’re one of the celebrity guests. For a night-in alternative, grab a bottle of natural wine at Bluebird Wine Shop, which is next to the cutest grocery store, Accord Market — I like to stop in and pick up pie or ice cream for at-home (in-cabin?) dessert and drinks.

Day 2: Saturday

Lunch

In the morning, grab a coffee and pastry from Black Dot Cafe on your way to a hike at Minnewaska State Park, which has many trail options of varying lengths and levels of difficulty. Alternatively, if you’re a climber, go to the Mohonk Preserve. Both are beautiful, and — crucially for our purposes here — close to a really great German restaurant for lunch. The Mountain Brauhaus is a scene. I’ve never seen the family-owned German restaurant not packed with people, and as soon as you’re inside, you’ll see why. The portions are massive; the dirndl-clad servers are charming and personable; slices of pumpernickel come with most dishes, and I’ve witnessed people try and then subsequently order a loaf to take home — it’s that good. Recount your jaunt in nature over a wienerschnitzel, some spaetzle, a wheat beer with a slice of lemon, and excellent people watching.

A Snack and an Activity

Skate off the schnitzel at Skate Time, a retro roller rink run by the people behind Bjorn Qorn. You’re here to skate, yes, but also to have some pierogies from Helena’s Pierogis (the pierogi shop’s brick-and-mortar location in Kerhonkson is cash-only, so it’s a bonus to me, a serial non-cash-haver, that you can enjoy them here under the glow of popcorn-funded lights).

Dinner

Westwind Orchard is a staple for me. I was one of those people who didn’t really understand the hype of a good summer tomato until I had a life-changing panzanella here a few years ago. The ambiance here is the main attraction — parents let their children run free in the fields, there’s sometimes salsa dancing and live music, you’re surrounded by apple trees. Still, the food is better than it needs to be and so what you want when you’re on a trip where nature is the focus: fresh, seasonal, and simple. Get the aforementioned panzanella and don’t decide between pizza or pasta; get both. I like the pappardelle and the seasonal pizza is reliably excellent (right now, it’s summer squash and blossoms). Westwind is a cidery, but if you’re like me and not the biggest cider fan, rest assured that there are also classic cocktails highlighting New York ingredients, like a Negroni Sbagliato with cider as the bubbly topper.

Day 3: Sunday

Breakfast

Head north to Kingston. Have a cortado and a frittata from Village Coffee and Goods, then make your way around the town, which is one of my favorites in the area and a shopping destination for antiques, records, vintage clothing, and books.

Lunch

Rosie General is my favorite all-day cafe. I always get a mortadella sandwich or a chile-crisp-topped egg toast here. Recently, I surveyed the room and realized it seemed like every sandwich had its own dedicated kind of bread (some on English muffins, some on ciabatta, some on baguettes) made in-house; I really admire that level of commitment to detail. I generally prefer an edible souvenir to a trinket, and the shoppy shop-esque pantry of homemade mustards, pickles, infused oils and vinegars is a great place to pick one up.

Afternoon Pit Stops

Many NYC people travel upstate just to go to Stissing House; us included. On the way, we discovered Zabriskie’s Waterfall near the Bard College campus. It’s a swimming hole, but the vibe is more lean against a rock and read. When happy hour comes around, check out C. Cassis. You might associate cassis with old-timey France, but C. Cassis is doing it differently. Here, the blackcurrant liqueur isn’t sticky sweet, and you can enjoy it in fun applications like a piña colada, while learning more about the ingredient from friendly bartenders.

Dinner

Waiting for your table at Stissing House is actually part of the fun, because if you come sans reservation, you’re offered a seat and a drink in a living room-like space with candles and serve-yourself peanuts. I happily sipped a martini there, humming music from The Testament of Ann Lee (it’s very that vibe, honestly), awaiting a dinner of ham and pickles, fish pie, and steak. Skip dessert here (it’s fine, but I have a better plan). Back in the Accord area, hit Cherries Roadside; it’s classic Americana in a way that I have to say speaks to me. There is ice cream, sundaes, and milkshakes, but I always go with vanilla soft-serve — enjoy while marveling at the fact that you didn’t have to wait in one of the absurdly long froyo lines back in the city.

Honorable Mentions (and Where I Want to Hit Next Time

Harana Market makes some of my favorite Filipino food in the United States; they no longer have a dining room, but watch for pop-ups or takeaway opportunities (or if you have a big enough group, get catering!). Eng’s Chinese in Kingston is a slice of local history; I’ve so far only gotten (great) takeout, but I want to check out its dining room next. I recently had a head cheese sandwich from Cafe Mutton, in Hudson, that rocked my world. And if you are wine-inclined, Kingston Wine Co. sells some of the coolest bottles in the state, and Mirador, also in Kingston, is a great spot for sherry and pintxos. I’m also dying to check out the Oaxacan food scene in Poughkeepsie.

There are too many places to fit in one weekend, so I made you a list of more favorites in the Eater app. Follow me for more of my curated picks from the Northeast. (Subscribe to our travel newsletter, too!)

items.title: 不评判好坏，只鼓励创作：这款AI原生游戏，让人人都享受讲故事
items.summary: 文丨寒刃
items.text:
文丨寒刃 二几


到了2026年，AI叙事游戏仍然要面对一个灵魂拷问：在完全自由的文本创作中，玩家到底该怎么知道自己要讲什么？


6年前，在《千夜之书1001》还只有基于GPT-2的雏形demo时，制作人起司就在尝试回应这个问题。如今，经过数年的开发和迭代，《千夜之书1001》终于为玩家搭起了一套“脚手架”，帮助玩家享受讲故事的乐趣。


《千夜之书1001》是国内最早一批试水AI原生叙事玩法的项目。故事背景脱胎于经典文本《一千零一夜》，玩家扮演的山鲁佐德，在与妹妹的故事接龙中意外解锁将文字故事中的武器化作实体的能力。玩家需要持续为AI国王讲述故事，从而制造武器，最终杀死残暴的国王。

游戏steam商店页面

最终决斗画面


对于一款把“AI对话”本身变成玩法的游戏来说，“让玩家开口”只是第一步。玩家讲什么，AI如何理解，游戏如何回应玩家的创作，都是《千夜之书1001》接下来需要回答的问题。


人人都能从讲故事中获得快乐


《千夜之书1001》的早期DEMO称作《1001夜》，体验非常简洁：


玩家唯一需要做的事情就是给AI国王讲故事，在故事中自然讲出含有武器的内容，并最终用这些武器击败国王。在这个过程中，AI国王会基于自己的人设背景对故事做出反馈和引导，意图过于明显的故事可能惹怒国王，直接触发处决结局。

游戏早期画面

处决结局


对于本就擅长讲故事的玩家来说，游戏的乐趣显而易见：与AI国王斗智斗勇的同时，创作本身就是快乐的。讲出精彩或离谱的故事，也颇具成就感。


但如何让不擅长讲故事，或疲于创作的玩家，也能享受讲故事的乐趣？起司表示，要给玩家搭好“脚手架”。


首先，游戏需要让玩家知道怎么开始讲故事。早期DEMO只有一句话的提示，如今游戏加入了“灵感卡”系统，可以把进入寝殿前的经历直接当做故事的开头。另外多周目游玩的玩家，还可以选择“故事书”续写上一局没写完的故事。

灵感卡与故事书界面


游戏还加入一项“辅助名字”功能。起因是起司发现，如果玩家把自己认识的人或者熟悉的角色写进故事里，往往会有更好的节目效果，于是干脆顺着这个行为设计功能。在北京Dice Con展会现场，有多位玩家以“牛来”为主角创作，引得众人围观，视频在小红书获得近400点赞。

展会现场视频


有了顺畅的开头，游戏还需要让玩家知道自己的讲述正在产生什么影响。早期版本中，国王的情绪状态是半隐藏的，玩家往往要等到国王生气，才意识到自己的行为已经改变了他的状态。后续团队发现，游戏可以不给故事的文本打分，而给讲故事中的操作加分，比如激怒国王或哄国王开心，一句话里触发了多个道具等。这样明确的反馈可以帮助玩家理解游戏正在发生什么，从而更明确自己下一步行动。


起司表示，这一设计的目标并不是鼓励“好故事”，而是对所有“讲故事”的行为做出鼓励。种种设计都是让玩家觉得，讲故事本身是一件有趣、值得投入，而且能够得到回报的事情。


所以《千夜之书1001》也对于玩家的各种“骚操作”非常包容。比如把“刃”这样的字眼写进“辅助名字”里，就可以轻易让国王再次提到这个名字，并触发武器。

国王的故事中出现了寒刃的名字


在起司看来，这些行为并不一定需要被当成Bug修复。只要玩家能够想到一种方式，利用系统让故事产生意料之外的结果，这本身就是一种游戏行为，也是游戏乐趣的一部分。


从“讲故事”到“玩故事”


最早的《千夜之书1001》是起司在博士期间的研究项目，还发了论文。但随着项目越来越大，想承载的东西越来越多，它也逐渐从一个实验性Demo变成了一款完整的游戏。这意味着游戏需要有完整的剧情与世界观，让碎片化的即兴创作，落地为有温度、有记忆点、可长线沉淀的游戏内容。


起司认为，自己在开发过程中犯过最大的错误，就是低估了剧情的难度。单纯复刻《一千零一夜》的故事是远远不够的，起司希望女主成为一个“真实存在过的人”，有自己的生命历程。

山鲁佐德的童年故事


在创作期间的大量废案让起司真切体会到，为什么业内都说“游戏的第二关最难做”。团队最初为女主刺杀国王的行为设计的动因，是妹妹遭遇意外，但这样的设定，会让妹妹没有主体性。经过与编剧的反复磨合，团队最终引入咒印的核心设定，让女主的抗争与救赎更有支撑，整体故事逻辑也更加严密自洽。


补全世界观和人物背景后，起司认为，如今的《千夜之书1001》，很像一个叙事游戏。后续剧情还会出现园丁、医生、将军等形形色色的角色；女孩们手腕的咒印设定、山鲁佐德踏上救赎之路的初衷，所有伏笔与留白，都会在剧情中逐一揭晓。

在故事中，女孩们的手上会浮现出咒印。当咒印变红，她们就会成为国王的“新娘”。

山鲁佐德与想要成为将军的童年好友


团队是从游戏里生长出来的


《千夜之书1001》的另一个特别之处是，作为一款AI原生游戏，它是随着AI的发展一步步成型的，见证了这个快速迭代的AI时代。


最初的Demo可以追溯到6年前起司大学时期做的一次课题，当时GPT-2刚刚流行。《千夜之书1001》的开发团队正式组建并运作起来，其实只有一年多。

团队简介


从学术项目到上线Steam，《千夜之书1001》的商业化没有一个清晰的“转折时刻”。起司认为，这更像是一种渐进式的生长。随着大模型逐渐成熟，行业开始出现新的生态，团队自身也不断成长，而这个Demo本身又逐渐证明了自己“值得被继续做下去”。


由于没有同类参考作品，项目自始至终没有固定的发展方向，甚至难以界定游戏的类型。团队依靠玩家反馈，一点点调整优化内容。早期，Demo还在作为学术项目研发，团队曾经研究过实时场景生成等功能，来让玩家获得更强的沉浸感和反馈。但后来发现效果并不好，玩家接受度也不高，于是直接砍掉。起司认为，这类决策更多是在不断与玩家碰撞之后做出的。

被砍掉的实时场景生成功能


同样，这款游戏的制作团队，也不同于多数独立游戏工作室。起司形容团队是“随着游戏的完善慢慢生长出来的”，而不是走立项、拉投资、研发、发行的路子。


AI技术的发展，也改变了团队的工作流。现在团队的非技术人员，也可以通过vibe coding制作玩法demo，甚至直接完成一些小型功能的研发。队内也形成了“show me the demo”的工作方式，策划提出新需求时，会先做出demo给到程序，简化沟通和开发流程。


这也正是本作最特别的地方：游戏、团队、技术三者同步成长，构成了《千夜之书1001》项目的核心底色。AI原生游戏本就是个没有成熟参考、固定方向的全新赛道，项目更新、团队建设、技术迭代同步进行，彼此相互影响、共同成型。


聊起对AI行业的看法，起司表示，如果不是技术乐观者，大概也不会愿意深耕AI原生娱乐。她认为未来token成本会持续降低，AI技术也会持续进步，整条赛道还有很大的发展空间。在起司看来，当下各类AI原生游戏之间，比起竞争，更像是互相陪伴、共同成长。


本文首发自“36氪游戏”。

items.text:
图源/企业

本文约2900字，建议阅读7分钟

作者丨欧雪


编辑丨袁斯来


硬氪获悉，离子阱量子计算公司维刻量光近期已完成超亿元Pre-A轮融资，由九智资本领投，正轩资本、瀚晖资本跟投。此前公司曾完成一轮天使轮融资，半年内连续完成两轮。本轮资金将主要用于产线扩大及整机建设。目前正启动新一轮融资，多维资本担任长期独家财务顾问。


维刻量光成立于今年2月，定位为离子阱路线的量子计算整机公司，核心业务包括芯片与整机、面向科研的真机算力服务，以及面向AI等场景的应用解决方案。


公司创始人欧凌峰为清华大学物理系博士在读，师从国际顶尖离子阱专家 Kihwan Kim，长期从事离子阱量子计算相关研究。公司核心团队来自清华大学、中国科学院及国内外顶尖高校，同时具备产业界经验，是国内国内最早做玻璃基QCCD技术路线团队，具备从量子芯片设计、制造到测试的全链条能力，并覆盖整机硬件控制、系统集成及应用落地。


欧凌峰向硬氪表示，目前公司芯片与整机业务相对成熟，已在实验室通过验证并开始小批量交付，应用能力仍在搭建中，公司也在考虑与软件公司展开合作。


与国内其他离子阱团队相比，维刻量光的差异化在于选择了玻璃基QCCD技术路线。欧凌峰提到，相较于硅基QCCD，玻璃基QCCD具有更强的通用性，同时芯片迭代周期更短，两周左右即可完成一轮迭代；而硅基流片周期相对更长，芯片制造耗时也更长。芯片性能决定了整机计算性能的上限，而芯片的迭代效率又直接影响整机性能演进和产品迭代的速度。


在核心技术指标方面，核心团队此前在清华大学实验室已实现由531个离子组成的稳定离子晶格，以及超过10小时的相干时间。这些长期科研积累正进一步转化为维刻量光在大规模离子囚禁、精细量子操控和QCCD整机工程化方面的技术能力。


欧凌峰解释，传统芯片此前需在低温下才能有较好性能，维刻量光通过工艺改良与芯片设计，使芯片在常温下也有非常好的性能表现，从而拓宽了离子阱量子计算机的适用范围，并降低成本。


欧凌峰认为，离子阱芯片现在已经到了工程化阶段。此前离子阱芯片依靠手工组装，无论是四级杆还是刀片阱，都是较大装置，依赖人工组装手感。现在维刻量光能做到同一设计、同一程序、同样工艺跑出来的芯片非常接近，具备“设计即所得”的能力。


具体来看，维刻量光的技术路线图是：现在做电集成的芯片，之后做光电集成的芯片，更后面做芯片之间的量子互联，往超大规模量子计算集群拓展。


欧凌峰用经典算力类比：经典计算机曾经很大，IBM、英特尔把它做小，英伟达再用板卡间互联把显卡算力扩展，相当于先变小再变大。量子芯片同样先变小再变大，光电集成是把很大体积的算力缩小，小了之后可复制，再通过量子互联扩展。公司提出从电互联到光互联到量子互联的路径。


值得注意的是，AI在维刻量光技术体系中承担全链条赋能角色。欧凌峰表示，从芯片到系统驱动再到上层编码，AI全链条赋能量子计算机。


在应用场景方面，维刻量光重点面向量子化学与材料计算、生物医药、复杂优化以及量子与人工智能融合等方向，具体覆盖新材料与高温超导材料预测、分子结构与反应过程模拟、蛋白质及小分子计算、组合优化等场景。


商业化方面，维刻量光已获得来自国内顶尖高校的订单，并正在与多家算力中心推进量子算力接入及联合算力服务框架的构建，探索将QPU作为新型异构算力单元接入现有算力基础设施。


欧凌峰判断，大模型的崛起正在重塑市场对算力价值的认知。未来，量子计算机有望成为算力基础设施的重要组成部分，与CPU、GPU协同工作，量子计算、人工智能与现有计算工作流的融合，也将进一步拓展新的算力需求和应用场景。


时间表上，他认为未来3至5年内，材料预测、量子化学和蛋白质模拟等领域有望迎来类似“AlphaGo时刻”的标志性突破；而更大规模的通用量子计算应用，例如密码分析等，可能需要7至10年。相比等待技术完全成熟，他更主张先让量子算力进入真实工作流，在应用中持续迭代硬件、软件和算法能力。


以下为硬氪与公司创始人欧凌峰的对话节选（经编辑）：


硬氪：AI在量子计算机中具体起什么作用？


欧凌峰：AI正在贯穿量子计算机从底层硬件到上层应用的完整链路。在芯片设计环节，公司引入AI辅助设计与参数优化；在量子态读出、系统校准和运行控制环节，通过自适应算法提升系统稳定性和自动化水平，将过去大量依赖人工经验的调试过程逐步转化为智能化闭环；在更上层，用户可以通过自然语言描述计算需求，由AI进一步完成任务解析、量子线路生成、编译并下发至量子计算系统执行。总体而言，AI正从芯片设计、量子操控、系统运行到应用交互，对量子计算全栈进行赋能。


硬氪：投资人目前比较关心哪些维度？对商业化进度有硬性要求吗？


欧凌峰：投资人主要看两方面：一是团队技术是否与要做的事情匹配，即人和事是否匹配；二是团队是否具备商业化意识，能否为客户考虑，这跟科研会稍微有些不一样。要求目前没有，因为这个领域还比较初期，技术路线时常会有改变，有时会与原先设想有偏差，投资人目前也比较理解。


硬氪：接下来的挑战主要在哪里？


欧凌峰：挑战主要还是来自技术和商业化两方面。技术上，量子计算还处在比较早期的阶段，怎么和AI结合，真正找到有经济价值、能落地的场景，还需要持续验证。


商业化上，这件事也不是产品方单方面把东西做好就够了，也希望需求方愿意开放一些真实场景，大家一起往前走。现在很多应用在原型机上跑起来没有太大问题，但真正有价值的是把需求、算法、真机算力到最终应用这一整套链路跑通。我们也在和一些场景方一起尝试，希望他们愿意更早一点参与进来，把整套工作流真正用起来，而不是等所有东西都完全成熟了以后再接入。


投资方观点：


九智资本：量子计算正处于从基础研究走向工程化突破的关键阶段，离子阱路线凭借高保真度、长相干时间和全连接操控等优势，展现出通往容错量子计算的重要潜力。维刻量光源自国际顶尖的金奇奂教授团队，兼具深厚的科研积累与突出的工程化能力，是国内稀缺的在QCCD架构具备系统布局的团队，已取得具有国际竞争力的成果。我们看好团队持续攻克底层核心技术、推动离子阱量子计算规模化发展的能力，也期待陪伴维刻量光成长为具有全球竞争力的量子计算平台企业。


正轩投资：量子计算是有别于经典计算的全新计算范式，有望成为AI时代全新的算力底座。以QCCD路线为代表的离子阱量子计算是目前公认量子比特质量最高、最具通用容错计算潜力的路线之一。维刻量光团队脱胎自全球知名的离子阱量子计算实验室，年轻且富有创新力，公司独特的石英基QCCD方案开辟了离子阱量子计算中一条全新的道路，极具应用前景。正轩投资持续看好量子产业，未来会长期携手维刻量光，将量子计算推向全面产业化、通用化。


瀚晖资本：量子计算正逐步从物理原理验证走向系统工程与容错能力竞争，未来真正决定产业格局的，将不再只是物理比特数量，而是高保真操控、逻辑比特效率以及规模化系统能力的综合表现。离子阱路线凭借高门保真度、长相干时间和灵活的全连接能力，在实现高质量逻辑比特和容错量子计算方面具备突出潜力。维刻量光脱胎于国际顶尖的金奇奂教授团队，在离子阱量子控制、芯片架构及系统工程方面具备长期技术积累，并围绕QCCD架构形成了较为完整的技术布局。我们看好团队将领先科研能力持续转化为工程化和规模化能力，在离子阱量子计算由“高质量物理比特”迈向“高价值逻辑比特”的关键阶段建立核心壁垒，并成长为具备全球竞争力的量子计算平台企业。

维刻量光成立于今年2月，定位为离子阱路线的量子计算整机公司，核心业务包括芯片与整机、面向科研的真机算力服务，以及面向AI等场景的应用解决方案。

items.title: The Best Way to Watch the US Open? In Ralph Lauren’s Suite With 20 Olympic Athletes
items.author: Yang-Yi Goh
items.summary: With all respect to Ben Shelton and Stefanos Tsitsipas, who battled it out in the round of 16 at the US Open on Sunday, the highest concentration of athletic
items.text:
With all respect to Ben Shelton and Stefanos Tsitsipas, who battled it out in the round of 16 at the US Open on Sunday, the highest concentration of athletic talent in Arthur Ashe Stadium that evening was 25 rows above the court in the Ralph Lauren suite.

In a savvy bit of cross-promotion, Ralph hosted a group of more than 20 pro athletes—mostly Olympians and Paralympians from Team USA, for whom the brand has served as official outfitter since Beijing 2008, alongside a handful of RL golf ambassadors—in their freshly renovated digs at the Open, where the consummate American designer has now been the official apparel sponsor for more than two decades.

Beyond the instant photo-op potential of having a crowd of strapping jocks decked out in head-to-toe Polo at the buzziest annual sporting event in New York City, the gathering was also a great show of just how many people could comfortably fit in the old-school country club-esque space, finely appointed by the Ralph Lauren Home team with saddle leather banquettes, oak floors, and hammered brass accents.

Weston Wells / Courtesy of Ralph Lauren

“It feels very Ralph,” said Maia Shibutani, the two-time Olympic ice dancing bronze medallist, as she sipped on a cocktail at the long, white paneled bar. “Very Ralph,” agreed Alex Shibutani, Maia’s older brother and skating partner. “It really reflects the scope of his world building.”

That extends to the food offerings, which includes full sit-down lunch and dinner options borrowed directly from the menu of Lauren’s vaunted Polo Bar in Midtown Manhattan, including a top-notch shrimp cocktail, grilled Scottish salmon, and probably the best ribeye steak I’ve had in years. “It brings a different level of elegance when you’re able to have a sit-down dinner inside of a suite,” said Jack Wallace, a three-time gold medallist in Paralympic sled hockey. “Any other sporting event suite I’ve been in, it’s always just a buffet and you’re making a little plate, so to have something like this, at the US Open especially, is a really cool experience.”

That night, though, the real emphasis was on all these high-level athletes getting to catch up, trade notes, and kick back together while somebody else competed for once. “There’s such a kinship,” Maia explained, “where even if you have different experiences, you understand the struggle or hardships that you had to overcome to reach this level. And so for me, I always feel like it’s the first day at the school cafeteria in a good way, where I just want to meet everyone.”

Gymnast Fred Richard, who took home bronze in the men’s team event at the 2024 Paris Games, was floating around the room, soaking up the camaraderie. “It feels like this great family reunion,” he told me, “but then we’re all saying, ‘Why are we not doing this more often?’”

And then there was the actual tennis, which many of the guests were, in fact, very much locked in on. Nearly all of the athletes I spoke to fell into one of two camps. Either they were able to just enjoy that night’s match as something totally separate from their day jobs, like Paralympic high jump gold medallist Roderick Townsend, who told me, “It’s cool to be able to be up here and have no skin in the game and just root everybody on and watch people give it their all.”

Or they couldn’t help but directly relate to the intensity and determination on display under the lights, like three-time Olympic ice dancing medallists—and spouses—Madison Chock and Evan Bates. “Thankfully it’s not triggering at all,” Chock said, “but when we stepped out there and saw Ben and Tsitsipas warming up, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, they’re so focused.’ I know what it feels like to have those jitters—that butterfly feeling right before you are about to go.”

“It’s something that's so foreign,” Bates added of tennis, “but at the same time there’s similarities and I’m just fascinated by their approach. I will always admire and appreciate that opportunity to see a master of their craft, whether it’s tennis or painting or whatever it may be. I love seeing people who are exceptional at what they’re doing, because I just feel like what it takes to get to that level is the same across all industries.”

One notable outlier? Paralympic swimmer Jamal Hill. “I wish,” the bronze medallist said, laughing, when I asked if he’s a big tennis fan. “I’m just an athlete in the sense that I do my sport and go home. I don’t watch sports.”

Weston Wells / Courtesy of Ralph Lauren

What do you like to watch instead? I wondered.

“Entertainment isn’t really one of my hobbies,” he replied. “I have a Spanish tutor. I’ve been studying Spanish for years. I take math classes. Calculus.”

Just for fun?

“Yeah, just for fun. Because in school, I was always the kid where being an athlete was plan B for me. Plan A was to be a nerd. Long story short, I didn’t cut it on the nerd side, so I had to be a swimmer… Life’s got to be more than sports, man. You got to have some style in there, too. We got to look good.”

Needless to say, everybody in the room that night did, in fact, look good.

In a savvy bit of cross-promotion, Ralph hosted a group of more than 20 pro athletes—mostly Olympians and Paralympians from Team USA, for whom the brand has served as official outfitter since Beijing 2008, alongside a handful of RL golf ambassadors—in their freshly renovated digs at the Open, where the consummate American designer has now been the official apparel sponsor for more than two decades.

Beyond the instant photo-op potential of having a crowd of strapping jocks decked out in head-to-toe Polo at the buzziest annual sporting event in New York City, the gathering was also a great show of just how many people could comfortably fit in the old-school country club-esque space, finely appointed by the Ralph Lauren Home team with saddle leather banquettes, oak floors, and hammered brass accents.

items.title: Public School’s Maxwell Osborne and Dao-Yi Chow on Their Epic Comeback, Nike ACG Collab, and Why NYFW Still Matters
items.author: Christopher Fenimore

items.text:
When I walk into Public School New York’s Garment District office, Maxwell Osborne greets me with a dap so familiar it leads a nearby PR person to ask if we already knew each other. “Nah,” we say in unison. There’s simply an inherent understanding between native New Yorkers like us.

Osborne and his co-designer Dao-Yi Chow’s shared reverence for New York City has always been vital to the DNA of their brand. The pair founded Public School in 2008 and quickly became staples of the local fashion scene, earning a handful of CFDA honors in the early 2010s and eventually becoming creative directors of DKNY. During the pandemic, however, the duo decided to shutter their label, before reemerging with a triumphant comeback show at New York Fashion Week this February.

A few weeks before their sophomore effort, last night’s spring-summer 2027 runway show, I was given the opportunity to browse through racks filled with the still-in-progress collection. I was thoroughly impressed with what I saw—a proposal for a complete modern wardrobe, full of familiar silhouettes tweaked just enough to feel genuinely fresh. There were boxy dress shirts, made in New York with luxurious Japanese cotton-silk blends, with large French cuffs finished with a single mother-of-pearl button in lieu of a cufflink. I spied wide-leg barrel leg jeans constructed in a patchwork of subtly different blue washes. My favorite piece was a pair of very long cargo shorts cut in tropical wool, with functional buttons that travel from the hems all the way up to just below the waistband. Most of the collection was made in New York, with some cut-and-sew done in Los Angeles and a few knits made in Italy.

I chatted with Osborne and Chow about how Public School’s yearslong hiatus helped reset the brand, their wild new Nike ACG collab, and why they believe producing runway shows in New York is more important than ever.

GQ: When did each of you first become interested in style?

Osborne: I don’t know if it was a specific moment. I was always into fashion. Growing up around the people I did and going to school, we always cared about what we wore, trying to be first on the scene with certain things. To really hone in on designing, that came when I was working retail and watching seasons come through the store. When it was quiet, I found myself doodling. That was the moment where I found out, like, “Oh yeah, it’s actually real that you can be a designer.”

Chow: I really discovered fashion and style through music. Growing up in New York City in the early ’90s, hip hop was such a big part of my life, and through the music I discovered the ideas and the power of style—not necessarily brands or clothing, even though that was part of it too. But it was such a big part of your identity and how you were viewed by your peers and kids throughout the city that it was ingrained from an early time in my life. From there, I developed an aesthetic and learned what things look good to me. Establishing that early on, I think, was a big key to now having a career in fashion.

Do you remember your first significant purchase?

Osborne: It was a pair of Jordans. Jordans at the time were probably the most expensive sneaker, and I was able to get a pair with some money that somebody gave me for my birthday. I had to fight my mother to get a pair.

Chow: I was also going to say a pair of Jordans.

It’s a New York rite of passage.

Chow: The Olympic 6s in ’92. That was the first pair that I ever bought with my own money. But I’d say the first piece of fashion was a pair of Prada [sneakers] in ’99.

How old were you at that time?

Chow: I was 25. The America’s Cup, silver, gray on white. It was like a group of us and we just went down to the Prada store when they came out.

Walk me through how Public School came to be.

Chow: Max and I used to work together at Sean John. That’s where we met and that’s where we established our friendship. It really instilled this aspiration of going further than people would allow you to or further than people think that you could, and combining that with growing up in New York City, having essentially the world in your backyard. That was a powerful time for us. We were able to travel the world at a really early age, and have a level of access that most people probably didn’t have at the time. Being able to go to Japan on research and development trips.

Osborne: We went to India. It was crazy. When I was at Sean John, I started as an intern and became an assistant designer at about 19, 20, and then taking development trips to India or Asia at 21, 22. The whole design team also took me under their wing and taught me different things. You’re seeing the world—New York is always its own world, but then to actually get to see it and be there firsthand, your eyes really open up.

Why take the hiatus and why bring the brand back now?

Chow: The hiatus was a necessary reset. We had been revving on all cylinders for five, six straight years of doing eight collections a season with the DKNY appointment. I think that we lost focus and lost purpose. The pandemic hit, and it was like, “Cool, let’s just take a season off.” The season turned into a year, and the year turned into fucking six. It really flew by, but we always knew that we would get back to it, and it was like, “Hey, let’s just take the time that we need to really get back to it in a meaningful and thoughtful way.”

Osborne: The reset was definitely needed. I think there is such a personal approach to what we do for Public School that when we’re doing all these collections and you come back to your own studio and you look at the rack, and you don’t recognize the collection on the rack because you’re too busy and you appointed a head of design... The company goes forward and you’re like, “Yeah, you have a business, but what is this?” Especially when we care so much about what we do. So that led to a slow down, to the hiatus, to now coming back.

How has the menswear landscape changed since you took the hiatus?

Osborne: Fashion has changed.

Chow: More men care about clothes than they ever have. It’s not even about clothes, it’s about anything that’s personal to them, anything that’s part of their identity. I think people nowadays have discovered how powerful fashion is as a tool to be able to align yourself with your tribe, or your group, or your set of morals, or how you want people to portray you. Naturally, the more attention, the more opportunity there is for new brands that come into the landscape.

I think with the rise of the athlete as sort of the muse, at least in menswear, you have a lot more cohorts [for men] to look at and aspire to or relate to. There are more access points and people are seeing it and incorporating it into their lives more than they ever have before.

As native New Yorkers, how do you feel about the way New York City has changed over the last decade or so?

Chow: The pandemic certainly reset the city. Obviously, a terrible time for a lot of people, but then you also had the real New Yorkers who stayed or didn’t have a choice to leave. All the economic recovery that happened afterwards certainly changed the landscape, accelerating all this new money and growth in the city, which definitely accelerated the gentrification of a lot of different neighborhoods. You had this push and pull of people who were born here, who built their businesses and families here, who had no choice to leave—and this new influx of money and private equity coming in, then adding their layer of what they think New York City should be.

Now, I think we’re going through a renaissance after Mamdani’s mayoral election. I’m a fan of his, and I think that he has really captured the spirit of what New York City is about, really helping all New Yorkers. Everyone lends a hand, everyone is part of a rebuild or helping each other get back on their feet. New York City is looking up.

Osborne: Ten years ago, the Knicks didn’t have a championship, so it feels like a whole different New York right now. It feels more united through joy and not through pain. Maybe it’s just us being lifelong Knicks fans, but it feels like New York is in a happy place.

How about style in New York?

Chow: New York City is a city of reinvention. That goes for everything: for your career, your family, your home life, and certainly your style. Most of our inspiration comes from walking, running, and Citi biking around the city and seeing people. So that constant reinvention—especially from the younger kids, looking back and making it new—will never stop. That’s what New York is. You have all these different influences that are hitting you at one time. So it’s like, how do you pull apart those different pieces and put it together and make it your own? And the great thing about New York City is everyone is doing that. That’s part of being a New Yorker.

What are some newer brands you guys are into at the moment?

Osborne: Some up-and-comers we’re paying attention to: Bryan Jimenez, Greg Laboratory and Zane Li.

Talk to me about the new collection. What inspired it? What are you trying to say with it?

Osborne: This new collection, “Living Proof,” is based on what’s happening in New York and the climate. We talk about what the new New York is and what the new uniform is going to be in the future.

Chow: It’s a discussion on modularity. The first show was the homecoming—looking backwards with all the codes for being introduced to Public School. Spring ’27 is more about looking forward and projecting out the uniform that New Yorkers and people who live in big cities need to wear. And all of that is dictated by the ever-changing extreme climates. Every time it rains now, there’s a flood watch. So you’ll see a lot of consideration to the elements and how extreme it has gotten, and really being prepared for anything that comes your way. Because that’s what New York is and that’s what it always will be: all these different elements that you have to deal with. How prepared are you to meet that moment when it comes?

Why do a runway show, when most brands are moving to presentations or showroom appointments?

Osborne: There’s something about the community that our runway shows bring together. It’s really nice for people to be in the same room. When we watch backstage and watch the people mingle on the screen, it’s some of the best feelings. We’re like, “Oh shit, our mother’s talking to so-and-so.” You can’t replicate that feeling when you do a lookbook. Those moments are very special to us and there is a sense of gratitude. We want to show face to people. We’re just locked up in the studio a lot, so it’s a chance for everybody to come together and to see the product move.

Chow: Also, it’s just keeping tradition alive. A lot of people here in New York have moved to show in Paris. So we feel a responsibility—especially when we were not showing for the past six, seven, eight years—that we, at least for the first few seasons, wanted to put on for the city. There is nothing quite like doing a show. A presentation or showroom appointments can never duplicate that feeling. It’s the energy that you’re capturing at the time, the people who come, the venue, and that feeling during Fashion Week. It was important for us to make sure that we came back and showed during New York Fashion Week.

These sneakers just arrived in the middle of this interview. What’s up with them?

Chow: These are the Nike ACG Air Max Goadome boots. I’d say probably second to the Air Force 1 Lows, they’re the quintessential winter shoe for New Yorkers. They came out in 2000 and were built for the mountain, but anything that’s sort of multi-purpose and functional and technical, kids from New York City have always co-opted that and made part of their uniform.

We wrote a whole Substack about this: If you were going out in the 2000s, you would see this boot because it was the unofficial boot of all the security guards at the clubs. Hopefully you didn’t get a close-up view of this boot in your face—that would probably mean you were not in a good place. But it’s really a staple of New York City street style. When you see this shoe, you think about nightlife.

When we relaunched, Nike was also relaunching the boots, so we brought them back on the runway. It’s so cyclical. The timing was perfect. We had pitched them this idea of trying to do a double monk strap on the boot, because we wanted something as an alternative to the sneakers that we were wearing at the time. We had all these really beautifully constructed tailored pants, so we wanted something that was chunky enough to ground those pants, and this was the perfect option for us. We’re super excited for these to come out. They weren’t even meant to be a commercial release, but the reaction to them when we debuted them on the runway was so great that the Nike team was like, “Yo, let’s commercialize these.” They drop on September 17th.

In an ideal world, where do you guys see Public School in five years?

Chow: We see Public School with a bunch of our own stores—certainly a flagship or a few here in New York, and overseas as well. We see a new crop of men who are really passionate about what they wear and care about the craftsmanship and the make of the garments. And a group of men who don’t want a bunch of logos and want to have a sophisticated wardrobe without looking like they’re trying too hard.

Osborne: All that.

Chow: New York City is a city of reinvention. That goes for everything: for your career, your family, your home life, and certainly your style. Most of our inspiration comes from walking, running, and Citi biking around the city and seeing people. So that constant reinvention—especially from the younger kids, looking back and making it new—will never stop. That’s what New York is. You have all these different influences that are hitting you at one time. So it’s like, how do you pull apart those different pieces and put it together and make it your own? And the great thing about New York City is everyone is doing that. That’s part of being a New Yorker.
What are some newer brands you guys are into at the moment?
Osborne: Some up-and-comers we’re paying attention to: Bryan Jimenez, Greg Laboratory and Zane Li.
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa306fcd511270de93dcf29/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/CF1_3497.JPG
blocks.c: Image may contain Li Daimo Clothing Pants Person Standing Adult Coat People Knitwear and Sweater

blocks.x: Talk to me about the new collection. What inspired it? What are you trying to say with it?
Osborne: This new collection, “Living Proof,” is based on what’s happening in New York and the climate. We talk about what the new New York is and what the new uniform is going to be in the future.

Chow: It’s a discussion on modularity. The first show was the homecoming—looking backwards with all the codes for being introduced to Public School. Spring ’27 is more about looking forward and projecting out the uniform that New Yorkers and people who live in big cities need to wear. And all of that is dictated by the ever-changing extreme climates. Every time it rains now, there’s a flood watch. So you’ll see a lot of consideration to the elements and how extreme it has gotten, and really being prepared for anything that comes your way. Because that’s what New York is and that’s what it always will be: all these different elements that you have to deal with. How prepared are you to meet that moment when it comes?
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa306fdbf1e02b5836afb99/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/CF1_3924.JPG
blocks.c: Image may contain Indoors Clothing Coat and Furniture

blocks.c: Public Schools Maxwell Osborne and DaoYi Chow on Their Epic Comeback Nike ACG Collab and Why NYFW Still Matters

blocks.x: Why do a runway show, when most brands are moving to presentations or showroom appointments?

Osborne: There’s something about the community that our runway shows bring together. It’s really nice for people to be in the same room. When we watch backstage and watch the people mingle on the screen, it’s some of the best feelings. We’re like, “Oh shit, our mother’s talking to so-and-so.” You can’t replicate that feeling when you do a lookbook. Those moments are very special to us and there is a sense of gratitude. We want to show face to people. We’re just locked up in the studio a lot, so it’s a chance for everybody to come together and to see the product move.

Chow: Also, it’s just keeping tradition alive. A lot of people here in New York have moved to show in Paris. So we feel a responsibility—especially when we were not showing for the past six, seven, eight years—that we, at least for the first few seasons, wanted to put on for the city. There is nothing quite like doing a show. A presentation or showroom appointments can never duplicate that feeling. It’s the energy that you’re capturing at the time, the people who come, the venue, and that feeling during Fashion Week. It was important for us to make sure that we came back and showed during New York Fashion Week.
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa306fc12a2c59cbd4ba060/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/CF1_3464.JPG
blocks.c: Image may contain Photography Adult Person Accessories Wallet Clothing Jeans and Pants

blocks.x: These sneakers just arrived in the middle of this interview. What’s up with them?

Chow: These are the Nike ACG Air Max Goadome boots. I’d say probably second to the Air Force 1 Lows, they’re the quintessential winter shoe for New Yorkers. They came out in 2000 and were built for the mountain, but anything that’s sort of multi-purpose and functional and technical, kids from New York City have always co-opted that and made part of their uniform.

We wrote a whole Substack about this: If you were going out in the 2000s, you would see this boot because it was the unofficial boot of all the security guards at the clubs. Hopefully you didn’t get a close-up view of this boot in your face—that would probably mean you were not in a good place. But it’s really a staple of New York City street style. When you see this shoe, you think about nightlife.

When we relaunched, Nike was also relaunching the boots, so we brought them back on the runway. It’s so cyclical. The timing was perfect. We had pitched them this idea of trying to do a double monk strap on the boot, because we wanted something as an alternative to the sneakers that we were wearing at the time. We had all these really beautifully constructed tailored pants, so we wanted something that was chunky enough to ground those pants, and this was the perfect option for us. We’re super excited for these to come out. They weren’t even meant to be a commercial release, but the reaction to them when we debuted them on the runway was so great that the Nike team was like, “Yo, let’s commercialize these.” They drop on September 17th.
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa306fca03792ace60dd8c4/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/CF1_3861.JPG
blocks.c: Image may contain Michael Rose Tom Wu Adult Person Pedestrian Cap Clothing Hat and Photobombing

blocks.x: In an ideal world, where do you guys see Public School in five years?

Chow: We see Public School with a bunch of our own stores—certainly a flagship or a few here in New York, and overseas as well. We see a new crop of men who are really passionate about what they wear and care about the craftsmanship and the make of the garments. And a group of men who don’t want a bunch of logos and want to have a sophisticated wardrobe without looking like they’re trying too hard.
Osborne: All that.

items.title: How to Massively Improve Your Bench Press
items.author: Dean Stattmann
items.summary: The bench press, star of chest day, has long stood as the de facto measure for a lifter’s strength. There are, of course, more holistic ways to measure
items.text:
The bench press, star of chest day, has long stood as the de facto measure for a lifter’s strength. There are, of course, more holistic ways to measure physical strength—and if your goal is simply to build muscle, you might not need chest presses at all. But if years of Hollywood montages have taught us anything, it’s that benching heavy counts for something.

To paraphrase Kenny Powers, not everybody’s trying to be the best at exercising. You need not worry if you don’t know, or care, how much weight you can put up on the bench. That said, if you know and very much care, we’ve got some intel that should have you stacking thicker plates on the bar in no time.

To find out what it takes to maximize the bench press, we spoke with top trainers, coaches, and practitioners who have studied the movement and understand the latest research. If you’ve recently hit a strength plateau, or even if you’re just interested in improving your form and efficiency on the lift, here are the experts’ top tips for taking your bench press to the next level.

Turn up the frequency

If you, like most men with lives outside of the gym, train your chest about once a week, you’re going to need to up that. “If you want to get better at bench pressing, you have to practice the skill of bench pressing,” says Luke Carlson, founder and CEO of Discover Strength. Just like training to run faster, that means attacking progression from multiple angles with at least two or three dedicated sessions per week.

To maximize strength gains and progression under the barbell, Mathew Welch, MS, CSCS, ATC, USAW-1, exercise physiologist at HSS, recommends a three-day training split that you can do on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

“The first day would be a maximal strength day, where we're doing 3–5 sets of 1–5 reps, because you can build strength through that 1–5 rep range,” he says. The second day would be for accessory work—to develop the surrounding muscles that play a supporting role in the bench press. These would be exercises like the incline press and chest fly, working up to two sets of 5–8 reps for each. And Friday would be back to the bench for what Welch calls a “dynamic effort” day. Here, you’re doing 8–10 sets of just 1–3 reps, using a load around 55–65 percent of your one-rep max and trying to move the weight as fast as possible. “The dynamic effort method can be very effective for power development,” says Welch. “If you're trying to break through a plateau, adding some power development can be very helpful."

Set your feet

Using proper form isn’t just about deterring injuries; it also makes your body a more efficient bench-pressing machine. “You can improve your form and technique and have your bench press go up, even though your chest didn't get stronger at all,” says Carlson.

“One of the most overlooked pieces of the bench press is really your feet,” says Jesse Shaw, DO, USAW, sports medicine physician and associate professor at the University of Western States. “Your ability to drive and develop force is really coming from your connection with the ground.”

The next time you’re about to lie back on the bench, take a moment to mindfully set your feet flat on the ground. And when you’re ready to pull the bar from the rack, make sure you’re engaging the connection between your upper and lower body.

“Your legs are really an important factor in the bench press, especially as it gets heavier,” says Welch. “You need to drive into the ground with your feet, almost like you're going to drive your hips up off the bench. Just being very stable and aware of the feet is important. It's going to allow you to use more weight, and it's going to help prevent overuse and injury.”

Get unstuck

When you find yourself consistently running out of steam once the bar hits a certain point (right before locking out your arms, for example), that’s what we call a sticking point. Essentially, it’s an indicator that one or more of the muscles involved in moving the bar need to get stronger in order to pull (or in this case, push) their weight. “Perhaps the limiter in your bench press used to be your pecs,” says Welch. “Now, six months later, it's your triceps, and you're having trouble with your lockout. Well, you're going to need to implement some special strength exercises to improve your lockout.”

If lockout is the area you’re stuck on, Eddie Baruta, global head of gym floor personal training at Ultimate Performance in Los Angeles, recommends focusing on developing your triceps. His preferred method: bench pressing with chains. While it might seem a little extreme, benching with chains is a simple and effective way to increase the weight of the bar as it rises, allowing you to isolate and overload problem areas. “You're actually increasing the resistance as you push through to the top of the motion, which we know is where the bench press gets more difficult,” says Baruta.

Alternatively, getting stuck with the bar closer to your chest, near the bottom of the rep, could signal a strength imbalance between your chest and back. “When you drop your elbows below parallel with the ground, your lats are going to carry that weight,” says Dr. Shaw. “So if your lats are significantly weaker than your pecs are, as soon as you break that level your lats are going to say, ‘I can't lift this weight anymore.’”

Lower the bar

Each rep has two phases: the lifting (“concentric”) phase and the lowering (“eccentric”) phase. While lowering weight may not seem quite as important as lifting it, research has shown that periodically exposing the eccentric phase of the rep to heavier leads can spur strength gains. Training “negatives” basically means lifting in a way that places greater emphasis on the eccentric phase of the rep. “You can carry a lot more weight through the eccentric phase of a muscle’s movement than you can through the concentric phase,” says Dr. Shaw. “Negatives, for me, are probably the biggest thing, especially if you have a weight ceiling to break through.”

To get the most out of negatives, Carlson recommends picking a weight slightly heavier than your one-rep max and, crucially, having a spotter or two on hand to help you re-rack the bar after each rep. Your aim is to lower the bar with control for a count of 10 seconds. Do that for one set of 6–8 reps, Carlson says. “If you did that every other week, that would probably be the single greatest way to improve your one-rep max,” he says.
